title: npm, packages and versions
summary: package.json, semantic versioning and ranges, lockfiles, scripts and keeping dependencies healthy.

sections.title: package.json
sections.body: `package.json` names the package and lists `dependencies` (needed at runtime), `devDependencies` (build and test only) and `peerDependencies` (the host must provide them, as plugins do). `scripts` defines commands run with `npm run <name>`; `engines` documents the supported Node versions.

sections.title: Semantic versioning
sections.body:
Versions are `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`. A breaking change bumps major, a new feature bumps minor, a fix bumps patch. Ranges in `package.json` say which versions are acceptable:

- `^1.4.2` allows `>=1.4.2 <2.0.0` (for `0.x`, `^0.4.2` allows only `<0.5.0`).
- `~1.4.2` allows `>=1.4.2 <1.5.0`.
- `1.4.2` is exact.

Pre-releases like `2.0.0-beta.1` sort **before** `2.0.0`.

sections.title: Lockfiles and installs
sections.body:
`package-lock.json` records the exact version and integrity hash of every installed package, so every machine gets the same tree. Commit it. Use `npm ci` in CI and containers: it installs exactly the lockfile and fails if it does not match `package.json`. `npm install` may update the lockfile.

Keep dependencies healthy with `npm outdated`, `npm audit` and automated update pull requests, and remove what you no longer use.

pitfalls: Putting build tools in `dependencies` and shipping them to production.

gotchas.question: What is the difference between `npm install` and `npm ci`?
gotchas.answer: `npm ci` deletes `node_modules`, installs exactly what the lockfile says, and fails if the lockfile and `package.json` disagree. `npm install` resolves ranges and may change the lockfile. Use `ci` for reproducible builds.

gotchas.question: Does `^1.2.3` match `1.3.0-beta.1`?
gotchas.answer: No. By default a range only matches pre-release versions that share the same `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` as a pre-release written in the range itself, so pre-releases do not sneak into normal installs.

gotchas.question: Why use `npx` or `npm exec`?
gotchas.answer: They run a package's binary from the local `node_modules/.bin`, or download it temporarily, without installing it globally. Global installs drift between machines; local tools are pinned by the lockfile.
